## Answer

**The Britannica entry on HEAT (E0090) describes heat in subjective, physiological terms — but there is no matched Wikipedia article to compare it with in this corpus.**

### What the Britannica entry says (E0090, scan page `page-1032-e28420685b47.jpg`)

The entry opens by defining heat as "one of the secondary qualities of bodies, produced by fire, and opposed to cold," and treats the sun as "the principal source of heat upon the earth's surface." Its core account is Lockean:

- "Heat in us is properly a sensation, excited by the action of fire; or it is the effect of fire on our organs of feeling. Hence it follows, that what we call heat is a particular idea or modification of our own mind, and not any thing existing in that form in the body that occasions it. Heat, says Mr Locke, is no more in the fire that burns the finger, than pain is in the needle that pricks it."
- "Heat, in the body that gives it, is only motion; and in the mind, only a particular idea."
- Citing 's Gravesande: heat in a hot body is "an agitation of the parts of the body... so that heat in respect of us is nothing but that idea, and in the hot body nothing but motion."
- It ends on measurement: "The degree of heat is measured by the expansion of the air, or spirit in the thermometer," and notes the same object can feel hot to one person and cold to another.
